title: Decide whether Eon agent workspaces need isolated execution targets
description:
## Why

Eon may eventually gain meaningful security and portability value if an agent workspace can run behind an attachable execution target instead of sharing the human host account and filesystem by default. The source discussion combines that useful boundary with agent dashboards, transparent container navigation, microVM lifecycle, and virtualized GPU work; only the execution-target decision is distinct from existing Eon workspace planning.

## Evidence

- Source discussion: https://github.com/luccahuguet/yazelix/discussions/685.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Product boundary` assigns product policy and launch to Eon, persistent sessions, attachment, and transport to Orbit, and native presentation to Venus.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Sequencing` requires Orbit and Venus proof before Eon composition.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Ownership rules` permits Eon boundary adaptation while forbidding duplicate child behavior.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Activation boundary` requires later slices to earn scope through dogfood.
- `eon-pxn` owns local Eon workspace topology and explicitly leaves remote machines outside its first slice.
- Apple Containerization runs Linux containers in separate lightweight VMs on supported macOS hosts: https://github.com/apple/containerization.
- microvm.nix provides NixOS microVMs across multiple Linux hypervisors and vfkit on macOS: https://github.com/microvm-nix/microvm.nix.

## Decision Contract

After the local Eon workspace slice is proven, decide whether one demonstrated agent-security or remote-workflow need justifies an execution-target contract. Compare doing nothing, a restricted host user reached through ordinary SSH, an existing remote SSH host, rootless OCI execution, and one platform-native microVM provider. Start from an explicit threat model and user workflow rather than assuming that containers are always insufficient.

If a target contract is justified, Eon owns target selection and product lifecycle policy, Orbit owns the smallest attachment or transport mechanism, Venus displays target identity and state, and the selected external provider owns VM or container mechanics. A valid decision may be to keep workspaces host-local.

## Scope

In scope:
- Name protected assets, trusted and untrusted actors, credential boundaries, repository access, network policy, persistence, and recovery expectations.
- Evaluate one concrete Linux path using exact primary-source revisions. EON-C7 excludes macOS/X11/Xwayland host implementation and proof; provider portability is background evidence, not Eon support scope.
- Define the smallest user-visible target identity, attach, failure, shutdown, and cleanup behavior only if evidence requires it.
- Determine whether existing SSH and provider CLIs satisfy the behavior without an Eon provider framework.
- Route any missing transport mechanism to a separately approved Orbit contract before Eon consumes it.

Out of scope:
- Agent dashboards or panels already covered by workspace and Venus planning.
- VM, container, SSH, filesystem, networking, credential-broker, or sandbox implementation.
- Literal filesystem traversal across hosts, transparent path equivalence, multi-tenant hosting, multiplayer, web/mobile, or automatic repository synchronization.
- Virtio-GPU, GUI applications inside guests, DRM Native Context, GPU sharing, or desktop virtualization.
- Claims that a restricted user, rootless container, or microVM is secure without a stated threat model and platform proof.
- Nova compatibility or changes to the first local Eon workspace contract.

## Implementation Notes

1. Begin only after `eon-pxn` proves useful local multi-session workspace behavior and dogfood records a concrete isolation or remote-target need.
2. Inspect exact revisions of microvm.nix, the selected Linux OCI or microVM candidate, and Ptyxis only for terminal-target UX; retain Apple Containerization as historical comparison rather than a required macOS investigation; distinguish OCI image/runtime compatibility from VM lifecycle and terminal attachment.
3. Compare no feature, restricted user plus SSH, remote SSH, rootless OCI, and one microVM shape on ownership, security boundary, startup cost, filesystem and credential exposure, recovery, Linux fit, dependencies, and removal cost.
4. Prefer direct invocation of an existing provider and an ordinary Orbit endpoint over a generic provider abstraction.
5. Record one recommendation, meaningful rejections, the evidence that would reverse it, and the cheapest isolated proof. Do not implement during this decision bead.

## Verification

- `br show eon-pxn --json` must confirm the local workspace prerequisite and its deferred remote scope.
- `rg -n "Orbit|Venus|Eon|transport|launch" docs/ARCHITECTURE.md docs/CONTRACTS.md` must identify current owners before proposing a contract.
- Every security and platform claim must cite an exact primary-source revision and the exercised platform; compilation or documentation alone is narrower evidence.
- The final Bead state must contain the threat model, ownership map, comparison, recommendation, dependency and tool impact, residual risk, and explicit user decision.
- No runtime, contract index, documentation, dependency, package, CI, or ambient user configuration changes during the decision.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if no dogfooded user need exceeds ordinary host-local or SSH behavior.
- Stop if the proposal requires a generic provider framework before one concrete provider proves value.
- Stop and request a product decision before adding an Orbit transport, security guarantee, credential owner, or supported remote-platform promise.
- Stop if isolation cannot protect the named assets without exposing equal authority through shared credentials, writable mounts, or host control.

## Maintenance Notes

Priority P4 and deferred pending local AgentRun dogfood and explicit user selection; `eon-pxn` is the related horizon, not a requirement to complete every unrelated epic feature. Decision effort M, implementation risk HIGH, confidence HIGH in the ownership boundary and LOW that microVM support will be justified before dogfood. Rejected as separate Beads: hideable agent panel because existing workspace and Venus planning owns it; transparent container-as-directory UX because it misstates the boundary; GPU virtualization because no Eon contract needs it.

## Docker VMM and Sandboxes evidence — 2026-08-12

- Docker announced the rebuilt first-party Docker VMM in public beta for Docker Desktop 4.86 on Mac and Windows: https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-vmm-public-beta/. The VMM is an internal virtualization layer beneath Docker Desktop; the same engine also powers Docker Sandboxes. Docker states that Linux support is planned for GA, but that roadmap is not current Linux proof.
- Current Docker VMM documentation records beta status, a 4 GB VM-memory minimum, manual host-directory sharing, absent Rosetta support, and known virtiofs/database limitations: https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/. Eon must not target VMM internals or treat beta claims as a product contract.
- Docker Sandboxes supplies the relevant product boundary: a standalone `sbx` CLI creates per-agent microVMs with private Docker daemons, filesystems, and networks; Docker Desktop is not required: https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/ and https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/get-started/. Current documented hosts are Apple-silicon macOS 14+, x86_64 Windows 11, and Ubuntu 24.04+ on x86_64 or aarch64 with KVM. NixOS support is unproved.
- Sandbox SSH integration is GA in `sbx` 0.37.0 or later. A named sandbox is addressable as `<name>.sbx` through an `sbx`-owned ProxyCommand, which is the narrowest plausible Orbit attachment path: https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/integrations/.
- The default direct workspace mount is read-write and therefore does not protect the repository from the agent. Clone mode keeps the source mount read-only and moves work to a private clone. Shared agent skills are also mounted read-write by default unless disabled, and local MCP servers execute outside the VM boundary: https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/security/.
- Sandboxes persist their VM, packages, Docker state, and agent state until explicit removal, and trade one VM plus one private daemon per sandbox for the stronger boundary: https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/architecture/.

## Current recommendation

Docker Sandboxes is the leading concrete microVM candidate only when dogfood demonstrates an autonomous-agent need for host isolation plus full Docker capabilities. Preserve the existing comparison against no feature, restricted-user SSH, remote SSH, and rootless OCI. Prefer direct use of the supported `sbx` CLI and its ordinary SSH facade; do not add a Docker SDK, Docker VMM API, Docker Desktop requirement, Eon-owned sandbox dashboard, mirrored provider state, or generic execution-provider framework. If protecting the working tree is part of the threat model, reject direct-mount mode and evaluate clone mode. Keep this decision deferred and P4 until one real workflow supplies the protected assets and failure cost.
design:
## Ghosthub-derived comparison constraints

Use Ghosthub 0.7.0 revision 072cc83559bd590ed5d759af05ec0a1868dbf359 only when remote SSH remains a credible candidate. Inspect its architecture, terminal-session contract, and threat model as comparison evidence; AGPL source is inspection-only and no Ghosthub, tmux, Herdr, or kwt compatibility is implied. These are decision gates, not adopted Eon behavior.

- Keep target inventory, liveness, and failures target-scoped. Cached rows may support navigation but never authorize attach, restore, mutation, or a live-state claim. One unreachable target must not make other targets unavailable or merge their inventories into one authority.
- Require a fresh owner-authored probe and exact target plus Session identity before attach, restoration, or mutation. A same-named replacement is a different target unless the selected provider proves a stronger stable identity.
- Keep detach, transport reconnect, target stop, and target deletion distinct. Reconnect must be bounded, serialized per target, cancelable, and non-destructive.
- Delegate host-key verification, authentication, effective route configuration, and encryption to system OpenSSH. Never weaken configured policy; invalidate cached connection authority when the endpoint, route, effective SSH configuration, known-hosts identity, or credentials change.
- Prefer no Eon-installed helper. If one is unavoidable, require an exact version for the detected OS and architecture, verify its digest after transfer, install it in a private per-user namespace, never replace a system binary, and define upgrade, rollback, partial-failure, and removal behavior.
- Keep credentials and interactive responses out of process arguments, environment, logs, durable Eon state, and provider-neutral schemas. Name the narrower unavoidable exposure and owner for each candidate.

Reject treating process names, cached output, or successful prior attachment as current authority; automatic enrollment of unknown hosts; retry that can create or mutate a target after the original one-shot authorization; and a generic remote-provider framework before one concrete target proves value.

## Docker comparison constraints

- Candidate interface: exact supported `sbx` CLI release plus its documented SSH facade. Docker VMM is provider-owned implementation evidence, never an Eon contract or dependency.
- Ownership: Eon may own target selection and lifecycle policy; Docker owns microVM, container daemon, mount, network, credential, persistence, and cleanup mechanisms; Orbit owns Session, PTY, and attachment; Venus may display opaque target identity and owner-authored state.
- Before selection, verify the exact `sbx` release, license and redistribution terms, CLI stability and machine-readable output, login and offline behavior, telemetry, behavior on the selected Linux/KVM host, stable target identity, SSH setup side effects, stop/restart/remove semantics, disk reclamation, clone/direct mount guarantees, shared-skill defaults, network and credential boundaries, and removal cost.
- Cheapest proof if activated: use a disposable repository and one named clone-mode sandbox; attach through the documented SSH path; prove exact target plus Orbit Session identity, stop/restart distinction, explicit removal, working-tree boundary, network/credential expectations, and cleanup. Do not install ambient SSH configuration or change host policy without explicit user authorization.
- Reject Docker Sandboxes if the demonstrated workflow needs only ordinary host execution or SSH, if behavior on the selected Linux host cannot be proved, if login or lifecycle requirements violate the chosen local-first contract, or if shared mounts, credentials, skills, MCP tools, or host control expose authority equivalent to the host execution being replaced.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The final comparison applies the Ghosthub-derived gates to no feature, restricted user plus SSH, an existing remote SSH host, rootless OCI, and one platform-native microVM candidate without assuming that Eon must support remote targets.
2. For every surviving candidate, the decision names the authoritative target and Session identity, distinguishes cached discovery from fresh liveness, defines same-name replacement behavior, and states what authorizes attach, restore, and mutation.
3. Failure and recovery policy is target-scoped and falsifiable: one unreachable target does not block other targets; reconnect is bounded, serialized, cancelable, and cannot stop, delete, create, or mutate work without a separate exact authorization.
4. Any SSH shape preserves system OpenSSH host-key, authentication, route, and encryption policy and invalidates cached authority after a relevant effective-configuration or identity change.
5. The decision either selects no helper or records exact helper ownership, OS and architecture selection, post-transfer digest verification, private installation path, upgrade, rollback, partial-failure, and removal behavior without replacing a system binary.
6. Credential and secret handling covers arguments, environment, logs, persistence, UI, helper transfer, and interactive authentication, and the threat model states any residual user-account or configured-host trust.
7. The user explicitly chooses keep workspaces host-local, defer, or authorize one separately scoped target contract. Closure creates no runtime, protocol, helper, dependency, supported host, security promise, or provider framework.

title: Rune: find and fix the 11-18 ms frame when a pane remounts into a fade
description:
## Gate re-scoped (Lucca, 2026-11-12: "yeah, we have to facilitate rune")

Acceptance is now the transitions Eon actually has, with no fade: popup show and hide, split and split restore, solo/zoom switch, and tab switch, each within 8.33 ms at 120 Hz, in two quiet-slot runs, with each measured transition shown to actually run. Eon on Rune does not fade panes in (Venus has no pane fades today; F6 was a spike test key). The fade-on-mount hitch (frames 120 and 202) becomes a Rune upstream issue body with its trace, written to a file for Lucca and not posted; it no longer decides adoption and exit rule 1 does not fire on it. Not a migration authorization. See rune-h-memo/MEMO.md, Gate re-scoped. The original text below is kept for history.

Rune adoption, bead 1 of 3 (plan: /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/rune-h-memo/MEMO.md; Lucca 2026-11-11: invest in Rune through a Yazelix fork that tracks upstream; "file all three now and start bead 1 in the Rune slot").

## Why

Rune track E (/home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/rune-spike-a-work/REPORT-E.md) found two frames over the 8.33 ms 120 Hz budget in all four quiet runs: frame 120 (F6 switches Solo(0) to Solo(1)) and frame 202 (a split restores). Each costs 10.9-17.8 ms of thread CPU, almost all in Rune's encode/submit; no Venus work runs and layout takes under 0.09 ms. This is the first stop condition of the adoption plan: if it has no fix, nothing of Rune lands in Eon.

## Do

1. Re-run E's unchanged audit (scripts in /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/rune-spike-a-work/, auditE.sh) on upstream anomalyco/rune dev head. If it passes there, record that and stop.
2. If it fails, split the cost with rune/frame-profile plus perf. Candidates: opacity-layer texture allocation (Rgba16Float at scale 2; render/upload.rs:187, render/layers.rs:444), pipeline creation, submission.
3. Fix it in the smallest place: in Rune (reuse layer textures, pre-create pipelines) as a patch for the future fork plus an upstream issue body with the trace; or in the spike's view code (keep the terminal element's identity across F6 and the split restore, as track G did).

Done when E's scenario passes unchanged (no threshold or allowlist change) in two quiet-slot runs. Time box: 3 hours or three failed approaches; then report and stop.

## Limits

Work in the Rune spike trees (/home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/rune-spike-a and its -work dir, or a fresh clone under /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/); nothing lands in Eon. Timed runs need a booked quiet slot (absolute gate). No GitHub fork, issue or post: write the upstream issue body to a file for Lucca.

comments.text:
Verdict: PASS — the final guarded Rune patch meets the re-scoped no-fade gate in two clean quiet runs. Claude and Codex re-checks converged, and cleanup is complete. This is not migration authorization.

Upstream fails the re-scoped gate: split frame 60 took 10.022936 ms in a clean slot. The candidate changes Rune reuse only for transient targets; cached targets retain their original policy. The scenario and every transition remain unchanged. Lucca re-scoped this bead on November 12 to Eon's actual no-fade transitions. Original E's fade scenario is unchanged and still fails upstream. The earlier retained-viewport PASS is withdrawn; neither that patch nor the unreviewed pool experiment is proposed for the fork.

## Numbers and measurement boundary

Upstream dev commit recorded at the start: `5fa472351acdbc33e16008f0ba3e816df67017db`. Corrected fixture tree: `3aee0029765fbff11bdf11a7d258ab0e5cd15593`. Final guarded candidate tree: `09acdd226611eba498ce1cbfa028176fb94622cb`. Final delivery tree: `972776c19e7bf17f348991f9a46c44232bfd6f80`; its only difference from the measured tree is the changelog wording requested in review. Both identity files pin their exact binary and historical Rune source, plus the common fixture, scenario, runner and checker. The candidate also checks its current Rune source against that recorded tree.

**Final alternating upstream/candidate/upstream/candidate batch, 11:53:48–11:55:01Z on November 12:** 930 virtual frames each at 120 Hz, 1920×1080 points, scale 2. All 870 frames from first input onward are measured, including input frames, focus-color animation, idle frames and final snapshot encoding. The strict budget remains 1000/120 ms.

- Upstream maxima: **7.184873 / 9.764771 ms**; over-budget frames **[] / [60]**.
- Guarded candidate maxima: **7.955748 / 7.782166 ms**; over-budget frames **[] / []**.
- Median run maximum: upstream **8.474822 ms**, candidate **7.868957 ms**. Only two runs of each are measured; this is not a statistical reliability claim.
- Minimum measured candidate headroom: **0.377585 ms**.

| Transition | Upstream 1, ms | Candidate 1, ms | Upstream 2, ms | Candidate 2, ms |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| split | 7.184873 | 7.139812 | 9.764771 | 7.069912 |
| zoom | 1.351289 | 1.151688 | 1.180098 | 0.990792 |
| selection-ends-zoom | 0.528520 | 7.077782 | 0.833361 | 7.782166 |
| zoom-selected | 1.161424 | 1.064125 | 1.148588 | 1.048849 |
| restore | 4.331452 | 7.955748 | 1.204483 | 7.604291 |
| popup-show | 0.814325 | 0.784053 | 0.641485 | 1.481162 |
| popup-hide | 0.840884 | 0.998943 | 0.563332 | 1.006690 |
| tab-switch | 1.737008 | 1.635671 | 1.619938 | 1.600619 |
| tab-return | 1.380704 | 0.740017 | 1.018648 | 0.827283 |

The table gives the actual input frame. The complete per-window maxima and all per-frame samples are in `transitions-quiet-results.json` and the four `.jsonl` traces. Windows last 90 frames, with 150 after tab return. All four runs pass nine positive witnesses and 36 negative mutations. No transition was removed or hidden.

`quiet-proof.json` records wrapper 1239327 exit 0, no foreign grants, all three locks free afterward and no active holders. The explicit grant was 11:53:38–12:03:38Z; the batch ended at 11:55:01Z, before its holder-drain/start cutoff and grant end. Builds, GPU tests and both reviewers had finished before measurement.

These numbers measure **Rune CPU-side wall time from frame start through queue submission**, with empty Venus effect slots. GPU completion/execution, presentation, PTYs and Venus terminal preparation/drawing are outside this measurement. The headless runner waits for GPU completion after the timer. This proves neither end-to-end Eon frame rate nor a real desktop's 120 Hz behavior.

Earlier evidence is retained: clean upstream frame 60 failed at 10.022936 ms (`transitions-clean-fail-1105`); an instrumented run reproduced 8.505522 ms, with 7.380288 ms encode/submit and 8.370192 ms thread CPU. The unguarded predecessor passed two quiet runs but introduced a cache-budget regression; its source, traces and identities are superseded in `transitions-rounded-unguarded-1116`. A prior unformatted diagnostic recorded 8.336752 ms, preserved numerically in NOTES.

The 05:47 pair was excluded for heavy overlap; the 06:32 slot was unused during product-fidelity fixes; the 08:50 runner refused to measure with a live holder at its cutoff. None contributes acceptance evidence. No failed or interrupted attempt was silently replaced with a pass claim.

## What the corrected scenario proves

The nine commands create a split, zoom pane 0, select pane 1 and thereby end zoom, zoom the selected pane, explicitly restore columns, show/hide a popup, then switch tabs and back. Every action must produce the expected mounted roots and exact rectangles immediately, persisting until the next action. The popup is an opaque overlaid card; both underlying columns retain their element IDs and geometry through show/hide. Hide and tab changes restore the selected pane's actual polled runtime focus, exposed by a small trace marker.

The checker reconstructs Rune's sparse element and channel deltas. It checks root rectangles and visible bounds throughout every window, all element opacities = 1, root scale = 1 and blur = 0. Thirty-six negative mutations cover no-op actions, fades, later geometry collapse and clipping; each must fail on its own transition. Pane focus is checked from two frames after each action through the window. Popup focus itself is supported by the explicit focus call; its marker only distinguishes “no pane focused,” so it is not a positive popup-focus witness. There is no threshold change or allowlist.

The unchanged generic motion analyzer and in-process gate remain diagnostic outputs. They flag the intended instant cuts/pops and Rune's focus-border feedback; this report does not claim they pass. The re-scoped acceptance is the explicit visible-transition/no-fade/all-frame CPU check. Original E's scenario, host and analyzer remain unchanged.

## Cause of the original fade hitch

Two uncontaminated 04:04Z upstream runs recorded frames 120/202 at **13.592358/12.404642 ms** and **14.125777/13.731869 ms**. Profiling attributed the expensive boundary to first submission of large opacity-layer targets, not layout, text shaping, pipeline creation or the synchronous texture constructor. Frame-profile encode/submit was 15.941/15.117 ms, with layout below 0.09 ms and zero text shaping. A separate strace run measured `I915_GEM_EXECBUFFER2` at 18.170/14.808 ms inside 18.933/15.630 ms submits. Newly used RGBA16Float targets totalled about 120/90 MiB at scale 2. Kernel memory backing/pinning is an inference; no kernel stack proved the exact mechanism.

`UPSTREAM-ISSUE.md` is the unposted issue body with the trace, evidence paths and limitations. The experimental warmed pool preserved the fade in one untimed run but cost 116.25 MiB and increased first-frame time; it has no completed GPU regression suite or quiet acceptance. It is parked as `pool-experimental-not-for-fork.patch`, not approved for the fork. The original 04:02 interrupted batch and its 986.448891 ms outlier remain excluded; their cause was not profiled.

## Cause and fix for the no-fade failure

Even with opacity 1, a header has an isolation target to composite its soft clip correctly. Solo uses a 3840×64 RGBA16Float header texture. Split needs two 1920×64 buckets. The old condition compares allocated area against twice the unrounded content area (about 1896×60), so it needlessly replaces the full-width texture even though that allocation is exactly twice the required bucket.

The split probes recorded two new header targets totaling 1,966,080 bytes. A separate instrumented run measured a 6.215304 ms submit containing a 5.566 ms `I915_GEM_EXECBUFFER2`. For transient targets, the patch reuses the full-width target for one split header by comparing against twice the rounded allocation bucket. Dimension checks and the 2× bucket ceiling remain. There is no new pool, API, startup warmup or view change. In the header case, retaining the larger texture trades approximately 0.938 MiB for avoiding its replacement. This is a memory/performance tradeoff, not free work elimination. In the final alternating pairs, selection-ending-zoom rose from upstream 0.528520/0.833361 ms to candidate 7.077782/7.782166 ms, and restore rose from 4.331452/1.204483 ms to 7.955748/7.604291 ms. Across split, selection-ending-zoom and restore, input-frame totals are upstream 12.044845/11.802615 ms versus candidate 22.173342/22.456369 ms. The patch lowers the split peak but roughly doubles the measured total across these three transitions. It is a peak-latency tradeoff, not an overall CPU-time reduction. The mechanism of the later spikes is not yet profiled; final alternating comparisons will be reported without hiding them.

The clean patch is `rune-layer-bucket-reuse.patch`, relative to the fixture tree above (the Rune files also apply directly to the recorded upstream commit). It contains the transient-only guarded condition change, comment, two focused GPU regressions and changelog. Cached-target reuse is exactly the upstream policy; broader pre-existing cache admission accounting is outside this patch. It is independent of `no-fade-gate-fixture.patch`, which adds the fixture/scenario against copied hosting tree `ae92fa22fa15201543901717483eb4e82b6a9978`. The clone preserves that hosting baseline and original E source.

`UPSTREAM-BUCKET-ISSUE.md` is the unposted issue body for this fix. The separate required `UPSTREAM-ISSUE.md` preserves original fade frames 120/202 and their much larger targets; this patch does not fix arbitrary fade-on-mount stutters.

## What eon-t1rtk should carry

Carry the reviewed bucket-reuse patch as a separate day-one Rune commit, with its issue body and GPU regression. Carry the corrected no-fade scenario, positive/negative witnesses and exact-frame CPU checks into the app-owned audit harness. Preserve the adoption memo's separate resize, clipboard and dead-key patch sources. Do not carry the rejected retained-viewport patch or experimental pool from this bead. Keep the original fade regression as upstream follow-up.

Migration, fork creation and outward issue posting still require Lucca's authorization. Nothing is landed in Eon by this task. If subsequent hardware or real hosted-terminal timing fails, profile and patch Rune under the revised exit rule; no agent drops Rune on its own.

## Checks and review

The final non-instrumented perf build succeeded after package cleanup; build-bucket-final.sh completed with exit 0. Both debug public-API GPU regressions passed after the final clean rebuild (22.41-second test build, 0.45-second test run): transient allocation reuse and red/transparent pixels after shrink, replacement beyond the 2× bucket ceiling, and a 64 KiB shrinking-cache-plus-second-cache case with stable cache hits. The test file is rustfmt clean; size checks report zero errors and 24 inherited warnings. Python compile checks, drain free/held/released-lock and grant-parser self-checks pass. The original broad Rune library-test compilation was stopped for excessive memory; no broad-suite pass is claimed. All temporary profiling probes were restored before the candidate build. All four final PNGs are byte-identical to the clean upstream output (SHA-256 `64c32cfd28b3a98253b46f08284036dc64868f86581870693c5a6ee5f9f23f82`).

Fresh Claude and Codex fixture reviews and step-1 re-checks accepted the corrected product behavior and geometry proof. The clean upstream failure then required a new runtime fix slice. Fresh full runtime reviews confirmed the old quiet pair and cutoff interpretation, but Codex found a cache-budget regression and Claude found higher costs on later re-splits. The guard restores the original cached-target criterion, restricting the rounded-bucket change to transient targets. The added budget/hit regression passes. Final alternating timing is complete. Codex accepted the cache fix and independently confirmed the final hashes, 870 measured frames per candidate, maxima and absence of overlap. Claude accepted the code, cache regression, comparison evidence and cutoff rebuttal; its remaining wording fixes were applied. No second narrow round was needed because the final changes are text-only. See REVIEW-LEDGER.md.

No Eon change, br write, commit, GitHub fork, push, issue or comment was made. Cargo clean completed through heavy.sh (wrapper 1268573, exit 0), removing 3.7 GiB. The target directory is absent; the work directory is about 619 MiB. The owned headless sway was stopped after checking its exact PID/environment; no isolated processes or work-directory mounts remain. Standalone binaries, traces, patches, issue drafts and hash manifests are preserved.

title: Reveal the current file in Files from Helix (eon files reveal, Alt+R)
description:
## Why

Lucca, 2026-11-02 ("does eon even have 'reveal in yazi' like nova?", then item 6 "ok"): Nova binds Helix Alt+R to `:sh yzx reveal "%{buffer_name}"` (nova/defaults/helix/config.toml:47), which shows the tab's Yazi popup at that file. Eon has no equivalent.

## Change

1. CLI first (rule 5): `eon files reveal PATH` shows the calling tab's Files popup with Yazi at PATH (its directory, PATH hovered). Move the live Yazi (`ya emit-to <id> reveal PATH`) rather than restarting it, so EON-C10's keep-alive Files state survives; start it when not running.
2. A default Helix binding (Alt+R, matching Nova) in a Helix config Eon ships under `<eon config>/helix/`, never overwriting a user's file; coordinate with eon-nova-helix-defaults-8zqa (which currently says not to copy Nova's reveal bindings: revise that line).
3. Check that the Helix in use expands `%{buffer_name}` in `:sh` (upstream 25.07 command-line expansions); if not, that decides part of the Helix spike.

## Prerequisites

eon-agent-parity-a9g0.1 (show, hide and focus popups from the CLI).

## Contract

New EON-C10 clause for `eon files reveal`; stop for Lucca's approval of exact text.

## Acceptance

Integration test for `eon files reveal` (running and not-running Yazi, missing path error); isolated installed check: Alt+R in Helix reveals the file in Files.

## Current scope and prerequisites (8ebdd69)

Lucca's 2026-11-10 comment 6322 keeps CLI plus Helix key in this bead; do not split
that outcome. eon-73g9d owns Neovim/other-editor guidance. Files is the tab's shared
Project/Files instance: runtime pair.rs:152-242 already switches screens through
`ya emit-to` and the quick-search socket. Reveal switches Project back to Files at
PATH without restarting or losing Yazi state; start only if absent. Inspect the
actual pinned Yazi reveal command and exact endpoint/instance identity. Keep path
bytes/spaces safe, never shell code; decide directory/missing-path semantics in the
contract proposal. Explicit Files navigation must not activate the desktop window.

The Helix defaults layer is still owned by eon-nova-helix-defaults-8zqa (unlanded).
Coordinate its approved lower-precedence layer; never overwrite user files or add
a second loader. Its rejection of Nova-specific commands does not reject this Eon
command. If no safe default key can ship yet, bring Lucca's "add these lines to your
helix config" recipe option back to the overseer instead of silently dropping the
key or forcing unrelated defaults work. Check Alt+R conflicts/configurability and
document the default if shipped. Acceptance covers live/absent Files, Project shown,
missing path without topology change, quoting, and packaged Helix key/approved recipe.
Exact EON-C10 approval remains required. Follow affected wire/lifecycle proof if a
new request is needed; one isolated Helix → Files observation proves the final route.
Portability: neutral policy; name native installed evidence.

title: Remove Venus's macOS unsafe code for the CPU and RAM chips
description:
## Why

Lucca, 2026-10-27, to eon-overseer: "but create a bead to remove unsafe later". He gave it when he approved option (a) for eon-mac-launch-kz4p.3.

kz4p.3 relaxes Venus's lib root from `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` to `#![deny(unsafe_code)]`. It adds one macOS-only `#[allow(unsafe_code)]` module in `venus/src/system.rs`: five Mach/sysctl calls for the CPU and RAM chips, each with a SAFETY note, using `libc =0.2.189` as a macOS-only dependency. The bin root keeps `forbid`.

## Goal

Venus's lib root returns to `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, with the macOS chips still working.

## Options (choose under the reference gate; recommend one)

- A maintained crate that wraps these calls in a safe API, for example `sysinfo`, which already uses the same RAM formula. That moves the unsafe code to an owner that maintains it, at the cost of a dependency (AP-DEPENDENCY-001: weigh transitive weight against owning five calls).
- Move the readings out of Venus. Eon Runtime, or another owner that already allows unsafe code, reads them and sends the values. That changes which component owns the reading and maybe a protocol, so it is a contract question for Lucca.
- A safe Rust binding that appears upstream later (watch `libc`, `mach2`).

## Prerequisites

eon-mac-launch-kz4p.3 landed. Native proof of the chips (kz4p.12), so the replacement can be compared against known-good readings.

## Acceptance

- `venus/src/lib.rs` is `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` again, and no `#[allow(unsafe_code)]` remains in Venus.
- The macOS chips read the same values as kz4p.3's approved definitions (VEN-C28, EON-C30), checked natively.
- Linux is unchanged.

## Scope boundary

No change to what the chips show, and no new widget.

## Current evidence and ownership boundary (8ebdd69)

The five-call estimate is stale. venus/src/system.rs:765-933 has the Darwin-only
allow module: aggregate CPU, brand, load, per-logical-CPU readings and VM/memory,
including allocated Mach-buffer cleanup. lib.rs:1 still denies unsafe; Cargo.toml:33
pins libc =0.2.189. Preserve all current native reads, bounds, error paths and cleanup,
not only the original CPU/RAM percentages. VEN-C28/EON-C30 are retired presentation
contracts: use current USAGE/CONFIGURATION/PRESENTATION feature definitions and
VEN-C16/EON-C7 native-host/platform boundary; do not amend retired contracts.
Related eon-7i3t9 and eon-agent-parity-a9g0.12 settle a shared raw sampler: coordinate
one owner before choosing a wrapper/move. No duplicate sampler or Runtime → Venus
dependency. New crates require the dependency comparison, pin and exit condition;
ownership/wire changes require exact approval. Native Darwin comparison covers
values and unavailable/error paths; compilation is insufficient. Preserve Linux.
Portability: isolated Darwin reader change with neutral consumers.

title: Decide how Ctrl+click opens path:line references from terminal output in the editor
description:
## Why

K4, second half, of ~/.cache/eon-agents/eon-ideas-work/ideas.md (Lucca's idea
request, 2026-11-09; filed by eon-overseer's "auto-decide" note).

Agents, compilers and test runners print `src/main.rs:42:7` all day; Venus
does not detect file paths (venus/docs/INTERACTION.md). Kitty hints, WezTerm
hyperlink rules, VS Code's terminal and iTerm2 semantic history open them in
the editor.

## Decide (numbered, with recommendation in ideas.md K4)

1. Which shapes: `path`, `path:line`, `path:line:col`, `path(line,col)`;
   relative paths need a `/` or a known extension.
2. Resolution and trust: Venus never opens files. On Ctrl+click it sends an
   EONW request "open reference R from terminal T"; Runtime resolves R
   against T's directory, requires an existing regular file, and runs the
   `eon edit` path (EON-C10) with Helix's `FILE:LINE:COL`.
3. CLI parity: `eon edit -- FILE:LINE[:COL]`.
4. Whether clicks reuse the running Helix (eon-bjov6) once that lands.
5. Batch the EONW bump with the next planned wire change.

Contracts touched: VEN-C5, EON-C10, EONW. Owner: Venus (detection), Eon
Runtime (resolution, launch). Prerequisite: the localhost half lands first.

## Acceptance

A recorded decision with contract text drafted for approval, and the
implementation beads filed.

## Decision evidence and failure questions (8ebdd69)

The localhost prerequisite is closed. Inspect exact source revisions under current
REFERENCES routes before recommending a mechanism. State detection/native-gesture
portability; Runtime remains resolution/launch owner. Decide spaces/Unicode,
ambiguous colon suffixes, invalid line/column, symlinks, stale cwd/missing files and
untrusted printed references. No arbitrary command, URL-as-file or input execution.
Specify whether T's directory means Orbit's live cwd or tab launch root; they differ.
These are questions, not decisions approved by this audit. Evaluate EON-C35/36 policy
only where the proposed request actually reads terminal contents; invent no new grant.

The running-editor proposal eon-bjov6 has moved to the accepted Editor popup work
eon-xodrj.5; evaluate that route. CLI and click must share path/position validation
and failures. Exact EON-C10/VEN-C5 draft stops for approval, with a then-next-free
EONW bump only if needed. Completion is a recommendation and approved follow-up
plan (or explicitly pending approval), not implementation.

title: Make the bound_io EINVAL test deterministic
description:
## Why and observed failure

Runtime bound_io_accepts_einval_only_after_peer_hangup failed intermittently on
Linux (a9g0.5, 2026-10-29; comment 4767). Preserve kz4p.25's Darwin behavior:
EINVAL is accepted only after peer hangup. Treat this as a fixture race unless
investigation establishes a product defect.

## Current evidence (8ebdd69)

sessions.rs:385 bound_io checks hangup; test :4830 writes reply, drops peer and
immediately expects hangup. A fork can retain peer until exec; CLOEXEC does not
remove that interval. Nextest isolates tests, so arbitrary CPU-load repetitions
are not a reliable reproducer. Sibling fix 8859dd7 and closed eon-7lxwu contain
retained-descriptor/shutdown evidence; 7lxwu native run 42828287094 at 84fe888 is
historical comparison, not this candidate's proof. Replace the obsolete 500-run
stress gate with a deterministic counterexample.

## Scope and plan

Runtime test/fixture only unless bound_io is shown wrong. Retain peer.try_clone()
through the first hangup assertion, then use the smallest explicit shutdown that
establishes intended peer hangup while preserving queued reply bytes. Inspect
sibling/native evidence for side/direction: local write shutdown is not necessarily
peer hangup. Keep live-peer/buffered-data EINVAL rejection and unrelated errors.
No sleeps/retries, blanket EINVAL acceptance, fork harness or stress dependency.

## Acceptance and verification

- Deterministic red with retained peer/drop only, green with explicit shutdown,
  sensitivity removing shutdown. No measured rate-drop claim without baseline.
- Queued reply remains readable; EINVAL succeeds only at peer hangup. Live peer,
  including queued data, still rejects it; unrelated errors remain intact.
- Focused supported check plus affected Runtime build, root whole-workspace
  pre-review suite and fresh review; fmt/clippy remain clean. Preserve the native
  Darwin execution requirement in the acceptance field, scheduled by overseer.
- Production bound_io change requires lifecycle/contract assessment, affected
  Rust/Nix proof and original native kz4p.25 check; Linux cannot prove Darwin.
  Test-only work needs no profile refresh.

No code/build/tests occur in this planning pass. Portability: neutral fixture/API
with a specific Darwin semantic check; no protocol or live-process restart change.
acceptance_criteria: - [ ] The test still passes on aarch64-darwin: one mac-proof.yml CI dispatch on the changed test (kz4p.25's EINVAL path exists only on macOS).
notes: prime-beads 2026-11-03: the test is now sessions.rs:3512 (bound_io at :394). Race read from code: the first assertion needs POLLHUP after drop(peer); a concurrent test's fork between UnixStream::pair() and that child's exec inherits peer (CLOEXEC acts only at exec), so no hangup and bound_io returns EINVAL. Same class as closed eon-supervisor-stderr-test-flake-ixne. Candidate test-only fix: peer.shutdown(Shutdown::Both) before drop; check Darwin semantics. Reproduce by looping the eon-runtime suite (concurrent forking tests), not the single test under CPU load.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Second sighting (eon-tab-create-launch-8tl4's full eon-test run, 2026-10-29): failed once at sessions.rs:2555, passed on rerun. That agent's likely cause: a concurrent test fork holds the socketpair peer open, so no POLLHUP arrives.

comments.author: prime-beads-2026-11-10
comments.text: prime-beads 2026-11-10: still open on the tree (runtime sessions.rs, the test near :3833 drops the peer only). Under eon-test the race cannot occur any more (nextest, one process per test); it still can in the eon package checkPhase, which runs the eon-runtime tests on parallel libtest threads (be9a23a). So the body reproduction (loop the suite) and the 500-run stress-ng acceptance no longer work. Use the red and green from 8859dd7 instead, which fixed the same race in a sibling test: hold peer.try_clone() across the first assertion (red with drop only), then peer.shutdown(Shutdown::Both) before the drop (green). eon-7lxwu (in progress) establishes natively what shutdown and a retained descriptor do on Darwin; start this after it lands.

title: Break Eon's output and input paths down from first principles and find the route to great performance
description:
## Why

Lucca, 2026-11-09: "we can take our time / we need good numbers / we can start a research agent to break things down from first principles and found out the way to GREAT performance". The terminal comparison (eon-benchmarks-xl2bp.6) puts Eon last of seven on output throughput (cat64 16.7 MB/s lavapipe, 17.7 MB/s GPU, against foot 115), and the multiplexer comparison (xl2bp.17) shows tmux inside foot about 3x faster than Eon. Benchmark results stay in beads until the numbers are good.

## Goal

A first-principles account of where every microsecond and byte goes on Eon's output and input paths, the physical floor for each stage, and a ranked, measured route from today's numbers to the top of the comparison (throughput, latency, frame time, memory), which then becomes implementation beads.

## Work (research and measurement; no product change)

1. Map the pipeline end to end: PTY read, libghostty-vt parse, Orbit's terminal state, frame production and encoding (ORBS/ORBF), the attach socket, Venus decode, grid build, shaping and atlas, GPU upload and present; and the reverse path for a keystroke. Name each stage's owner and contract.
2. Measure each stage's cost per MiB and per frame on the eon-bench corpora (perf, the existing EON_BENCH_TRACE counters, headless Sway launcher, lavapipe and renderD128), detached and attached, with a quiet window per timed run. State the floor for each stage (PTY and memcpy bandwidth, parser throughput alone, the cost of one damaged row vs a full grid).
3. Study how the fastest terminals reach their numbers, from the clones in ~/pjs/refs (ghostty-7501, kitty, wezterm, rio, foot if cloned, alacritty if cloned, herdr, tmux, zellij): renderer thread and mailbox coalescing, damage tracking, frame pacing tied to vsync, how a multiplexer server sends incremental updates. Reference only; nothing is copied.
4. Recommend: the design changes, each with its measured or derived gain, its cost, and the contracts it touches (ORB-C4 frame ordering, the ORBS/ORBF wire, VEN-C contracts); a target number per benchmark; and an ordered list of implementation beads. eon-orbit-coalesce-gu13n is the first candidate; say whether its design should change. Fold in eon-renderer-gpui-rune-xsvwn's question 2 (where the attached-window time goes).

## Done when

A report in the bead's records with the stage budget table (measured), the floors, the reference-terminal findings with file:line citations, and the ranked plan; Lucca has read it and decided which beads to file.

title: Test that left-out Eon Bar items are never read and never wake Venus
description:
## Why

eon-vn0nk (2026-10-31) retired VEN-C29 (Eon Bar item order) as a feature. VEN-C29 said "Venus neither reads nor wakes for a left-out CPU, RAM or clock". That rule is now documented in venus/docs/PRESENTATION.md (Eon Bar, item order) and carried by the gating code at venus/src/application.rs:4739 ("Items Eon leaves out of the bar are never read and never wake Venus."). No test checks it. `eon_orders_and_omits_bar_items` (venus/src/accessibility.rs:1798), the test VEN-C29 cited, checks only the scene: chip order and missing nodes. The gap predates eon-vn0nk. eon-overseer agreed (2026-10-31) that it becomes a test, not a contract clause.

## Scope

In scope: one focused Venus test in the existing suite. When the bar items leave out `cpu`, `ram` or `clock`, the tick path reads no CPU, RAM or clock value and schedules no wake for it: `next_clock` and `next_reading` stay unset. Prefer the smallest seam the code already has. If the check needs a new seam, keep it private to the module.

Out of scope: any behavior change, any contract text, and redesigning the tick loop.

## Acceptance

- A test that fails if the gating at application.rs:4739 is removed (shown red/green), and passes on edge.
- `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings` stay green for the venus crate.

## Verification

One owned logic regression: the focused red/green check plus the venus crate build, via `nix develop -c eon-test -p yazelix-venus <test>`. It changes a test, so Codex reviews it.

## Current gate and falsifier (8ebdd69)

Gate: application.rs:6470-6526; wake-deadline assembly :6584-6587. next_reading is
shared by CPU or RAM. Omitting CPU while RAM shows must still schedule RAM, and
vice versa: test each read independently, then omit both to require next_reading
unset. Omit clock for next_clock unset. Visible due chips still read. Never assert
that unrelated shown widgets schedule no wakes. The same gate includes disk and
next_disk: cover its omitted branch alongside the original three, without new
sampler behavior. Use a minimal private seam only if necessary and exercise the
real decision consumed by the tick path; sensitivity removes/bypasses its visibility
gate. No public harness/loop redesign. Accessibility scene tests cannot prove no
reads/wakes. Use current test-change proof/review and root pre-review eon-test plus
affected Venus build; no installed refresh for a test-only change.
Portability: neutral scheduling; no real display required.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: prime-beads 2026-11-12: Refreshed gate evidence and corrected shared CPU/RAM deadline semantics, with the same disk branch covered by the focused test. Planning only; approved decisions and issue status preserved.

title: Decide what Eon does when a terminal rings the bell (BEL)

title: Benchmark Eon the way people benchmark Ghostty, Rex and other terminals
description:
## Why

Lucca, 2026-11-07: "we need a benchmark epic. we need to check on the internet and on x what benchmarks are people using, especially mitchell hashimoto on ghostty / rex". Eon renders libghostty-vt terminals (Orbit) in a wgpu client (Venus) behind a supervisor; people will compare it with Ghostty, Rex (Superlogical, Hashimoto's libghostty multiplexer, our fiercest competitor), kitty, WezTerm, Alacritty, tmux and Zellij. At filing Eon had scattered perf beads (Venus scroll baseline eon-venus-scroll-text-baseline-juo5, row text cache gxb4, blink rebuild h222, supervisor responsiveness pimct, remote paging 52i4.9) but no shared benchmark suite, no numbers to cite, and no regression gate (AP-PERF-001).

## Original goal (publication superseded below)

A repeatable benchmark suite for Eon that measures what users and competitors measure, run the same way against Eon and a few reference terminals, with published numbers and a regression check, before the v0.2.0 announcement if it proves cheap enough, otherwise right after.

## Original research/split order (historical)

1. Research (first child): what benchmarks people use now, on the web and on X, especially Hashimoto for Ghostty and Rex: tools (e.g. vtebench, Ghostty's src/benchmark and its CLI, termbench, kitty's benchmark, typometer-style latency, frame pacing), workloads (throughput of large output, scrolling, Unicode and graphemes, SGR-heavy output, alternate screen apps, resize, many panes), metrics (input latency, frame time, throughput, memory per terminal, startup), and how they publish results. Output: a recommended Eon suite and the child beads to build it.
2. Build the suite in small slices; the first slices measure Orbit throughput and Venus frame time on Linux, then input latency, then macOS.
3. A regression gate in CI or the proof routes, and a results page for the announcement or the website.


## Current decisions and acceptance (2026-11-12)

Research .1, harness/kernel floor .2, throughput .4, memory .5/.18, comparison .6, gate .7 and
mux/window memory .17 are delivered. eon/tools/eon-bench/src/main.rs:20-29 at 2e93c69 exposes
existing suites; the no-suite/no-gate claim above is historical. Remaining children keep their scope.

Lucca's 2026-11-07 "this is pre 0.2" superseded "if cheap enough, otherwise right after"; the
selected child blockers of eon-igae.9 gate beta, not this whole epic. His 2026-11-09 "we dont need
to publish, we can fix this before pushing / we can save it only to beads" supersedes publication:
.8 records shipping-candidate results after selected fixes; .21 retains page/charts/site scope for
a later choice to publish. His 2026-11-10 "yeah" made .9 → .10 → juo5 → gxb4 and h222 P1;
measure before redesign, with final frame/idle results in .8. No added startup/attach benchmark:
that remains an idea. No published keystroke-latency number from software probes alone.

Storage is settled (overseer, 2026-11-09, Lucca's "auto-decide"): /home/lucca/pjs/eon-evidence/<bead>/
for raw archives, result identities/SHA-256s in Beads. Already-pushed docs/benchmarks evidence stays;
no new repository growth or publication.

Every child closes or is explicitly moved out with a recorded reason; retain later chosen suites.
Beta metrics trace to complete durable evidence on the shipping candidate, naming revision/artifact,
machine, workload, compositor/renderer, runs/statistic/limits and fix beads where Eon trails.
Completion/CPU timing is not display/keystroke latency. Code proof stays with children under root
rules; timing requires a coordinator-approved quiet window and private roots, never Lucca's window.
This parent refresh verifies Beads state/graph, not runtime or performance.

title: Research the benchmarks people use for terminals, especially Hashimoto's for Ghostty and Rex, and recommend Eon's suite
description:
## Why

First child of the benchmark epic. Lucca, 2026-11-07: "check on the internet and on x what benchmarks are people using, especially mitchell hashimoto on ghostty / rex".

## Deliverable (research only; no product code)

A report with sources (URLs, X post links, dates) covering:
1. What Mitchell Hashimoto and the Ghostty project use and publish: Ghostty's in-repo benchmark tooling (a clone is at ~/pjs/refs/ghostty-7501/repo, see src/benchmark/ and its AGENTS.md), the ghostty CLI benchmark commands, vtebench or others they cite, how they report results (blog posts, release notes, X posts), and anything Rex/Superlogical has said or shown about performance (latency, throughput, memory, remote).
2. What other terminals and multiplexers use: Alacritty (vtebench), kitty (its benchmark kitten), WezTerm, foot, Rio, Zellij, tmux; latency tools (typometer, Is It Snappy, the "terminal latency" articles), and well-known comparisons people share on X, Hacker News or Reddit in 2025-2026.
3. Which of these fit Eon's architecture (Orbit host with libghostty-vt, the ORBF frame stream, Venus wgpu rendering, the supervisor), what each would measure in Eon, and how to run Eon and reference terminals the same way on Linux (headless or isolated display) and later macOS.
4. A recommended Eon benchmark suite (workloads, metrics, tools, harness shape, where results are stored, what becomes a regression gate) and a list of small child beads to build it, in order, each one session.

Existing Eon perf beads to fold in or link: eon-venus-scroll-text-baseline-juo5, eon-venus-row-text-cache-gxb4, eon-venus-blink-no-rebuild-h222, eon-pimct, eon-remote-workspaces-52i4.9. Competitor notes: ~/pjs/refs/WATCHLIST.md, ~/pjs/refs/competitor-audit-2026-10/rex.md.

title: Measure Orbit's key-to-frame echo latency without a display
description:
Child of the benchmark epic (Lucca, 2026-11-07: benchmarks are pre 0.2). Research and suite design: eon-benchmarks-xl2bp.1, ~/.cache/eon-agents/eon-bench-1-work/bead/ (04-recommended-suite.md, 05-children.md). Common checks for every code child are listed at the top of 05-children.md. Which children gate v0.2.0 is Lucca's call; see the epic's comments.

Add the `echo` suite: with the real-PTY test client's attach and key path, send
a key to a raw-echo child and time until a frame containing the echo arrives;
compare with the same echo through a bare PTY. Idle and with a neighbouring
terminal running `cat64`. Report p50/p95/p99 over ≥1,000 keys with random
spacing (thume.ca's jitter, so samples do not lock to a period).
- Checks: common; recorded table with the bare-PTY floor.
- Predecessor: C3.

## Acceptance details

Use the canonical Orbit attach/key codec and full frame revisions (ORB-C3/ORB-C4/ORB-C6
unchanged). For each unique probe, the matching authoritative frame must contain its echo;
exclude stale/previous echoes and report missing or timed-out probes as failures, never successful
latency samples. Apply the same raw-echo child and monotonic timing endpoints to the bare-PTY
floor. Report idle and neighbouring-cat64 distributions separately, including p50/p95/p99,
at least 1,000 keys and the jitter seed/schedule. This is key-to-authoritative-frame delivery,
not compositor presentation or physical keypress-to-pixel latency. Document the `echo` command
and result fields and retain a focused falsifier for wrong/missing echo correlation.

## Execution and proof boundary (2026-11-12)

Owner: eon-bench; this adds measurement, not a product latency/throughput guarantee. Reuse
the existing suite/result/environment/corpus/isolation owners; any new bench-only dependency
or Nix wiring records its reference/dependency decision before implementation. Keep it outside
the product closure. Source/CLI changes get focused meaningful checks, whole-workspace
`nix develop -c eon-test` before converge, affected build/Nix proof, and the existing frame/timing
route if the output path changes. Do not run suites directly in a live Eon environment.

Record exact candidate and harness revisions/artifacts, command, workload/grid, sample count,
statistics, machine/load and limitations. Obtain a coordinator quiet window for timings; use
private roots and clean up only owned processes without moving the desktop's focus. Raw evidence
goes under `/home/lucca/pjs/eon-evidence/<bead>/`, with artifact identities/SHA-256s and results

# Multiplexer overhead and one-window memory on private Sway

2026-11-09; eon-benchmarks-xl2bp.17. Native-VT status-reply time and process PSS: **lower is better**. Throughput: **higher is better**.

In the Intel hardware cohort, cat64 median native-VT status-reply completion took 2.40× bare foot with tmux, 3.37× with Zellij, and 6.37× in Eon. Filled-window median PSS was 105.0 MiB for Eon (70.0 MiB of it Venus), 15.6 MiB for foot and 174.9 MiB for Ghostty. Eon’s window includes its default Files pane: two terminals, Yazi and fzf. The tables retain both renderer cohorts and their distributions. Mux ratios may understate total mux-plus-foot cost because foot’s redraw work is mostly outside the timer.

These are fresh application launches on the terminals suite’s private headless Sway rig. Multiplexer overhead compares bare foot, tmux inside foot, Zellij inside foot and Eon in the same interleaved cohort. Per-window memory compares complete Eon, foot and Ghostty application process trees; Venus alone is a separate attribution row.

The recorded source tree is `de3676248d4271220115306b9cc4263063f7a0e7`, with immutable executable identities below. Review-fixed source is `b0efec76ea869d37513e401403c2b5b2942899a3`: it bounds Zellij startup by launching inside foot, adds attribution checks/tests, and corrects labels and method wording. It preserves the go boundary, workload payloads, timer and counter sums. Per the overseer's review instructions, those fixes require code/build proof but no replacement recorded cohorts; the tables retain their original source identity and values.

Every cell has ten measured launches after two excluded warmups. Subjects rotate within each workload. The inner PTY is verified at 80×24 before go and after completion; the grid settles for one second before go. All select the same pinned DejaVu Sans Mono regular file at 16 logical pixels (12 points at 96 DPI), SHA256 `9d9bfebceb1c3f6f4ad383ded568a6926086208f43f7f92f92f7e93a1383fa38`. Sway is 1280×800 at scale 1. CPU affinity is 2,4,6,8; a coordinator-granted quiet window holds other new heavy runs. Natural load remains in every sample’s evidence; this is a warm host with fresh private application state, not a cold boot.

Throughput uses the shared exact 64 MiB cat64 corpus and the pinned kitten render workloads, ten repetitions each. The timer stops when foot answers the status reply for bare foot, tmux or Zellij answers for its respective mux row, or Orbit answers for Eon. Rendering remains enabled. Foot’s work on the mux’s redraws is mostly outside this timer, so the reported mux overhead may understate the cost of the mux and foot together. Venus presentation is not awaited either. These are native-VT status-reply completion times, not delivery of the last pixel or input latency. Kitten reports rounded times and rates, so its inferred bytes and small differences have limited precision. Images measures protocol consumption; image-display support is not validated. MB/s divides the median inferred/exact byte count by median completion time. Overhead is `100 × (subject median seconds / same-cohort bare-foot median seconds − 1)`. This is an application comparison, with no isolated mux or renderer causal claim.

The shared setup first prints EON BENCH READY. Empty then clears the setup to leave a blank viewport; filled writes 10,000 numbered 72-column lines. Each waits for a status reply, then settles for one second. Only Eon’s screen content is checked in code, through an untimed eon pane read before that settle. Foot/Ghostty have no programmatic screen-content oracle; representative retained captures are inspected visually. Eon alone receives that pre-collection CLI read. Memory samples store rollup collection time in seconds, not status-reply time or output throughput. History is preserved for collection. History budgets remain distinct: Eon and Ghostty 16 MiB; foot and the inner muxes 10,000 lines. These are configured products, not an equal-retention experiment. The held workload subtree is excluded. Eon’s supervisor, Venus, Orbit hosts/Bend workers and support processes count; foot/Ghostty’s application descendants count. Every measured Eon tree includes the supervisor, Venus, two Orbit host/worker pairs (workload and Files), Yazi and fzf. Driver, Sway and D-Bus do not. All included rollups report zero SwapPss. PID/start-time and full process-set stability are checked around collection. Each fresh tree represents one window, not a marginal second-window slope and not the 50-terminal native-client attachment delta (`docs/benchmarks/venus-client-memory-2026-11-08.md`). PSS is primary; summed RSS double-counts shared pages. Ranges are nearest-rank p05–p95 (min–max at n=10). PSS depends on shared mappings on the warm host, includes mapped graphics allocations and excludes GPU memory outside process mappings. Fresh launches establish no long-term growth or leak bound.

This refreshes the September COSMIC report (`docs/benchmarks/eon-zlf-2026-09-08.md`) with a separate 80×24/private-Sway cohort. Its former 120×30 geometry, packages, compositor and product behavior differ; the two reports do not establish a memory regression.

title: Keep eon-bench terminals robust when Herdr fails early or the load wait runs long
description:
Non-blocking findings from the round-2 Opus re-check of eon-benchmarks-xl2bp.6 (log /home/lucca/.local/state/rota/runs/benchterminals-recheck-claude-u-1/log), left for a follow-up so the reviewed harness and its recorded cohorts could land. None changes the published numbers: they affect failure paths only.

1. A Herdr failure can abort the whole run. The herdr-core stop guard now also runs on Herdr's early errors (version probe, compositor start, the app exiting before the core comes up). If `hc server stop` exits non-zero when no server is running, it writes core-stop-failure.txt and run_inner (terminals.rs:664) aborts everything instead of recording a Herdr gap. Treat "no server to stop" as success, or only arm the guard once the core is up.
2. The load wait spends the per-sample deadline (terminals.rs:1449). A long but successful wait for load can leave too little time for the workload, and the overrun becomes a subject failure (a gap for Herdr). Keep the load wait outside the sample deadline, bounded by its own --load-wait limit, while startup and workload still share one deadline (Codex's round-1 finding 3).
3. docs/DEVELOPMENT.md:584 lists the compared terminals without Herdr.
4. Historical review finding: the old load-deadline test only re-checked map_err. At 8ebdd69, `a_short_load_deadline_remains_an_environment_failure` (terminals.rs:1934) calls the real wait path and checks classification/bounded failure. Keep that coverage; add the missing successful-long-wait case against the actual sample deadline path.

Acceptance: fixes with focused tests, eon-bench suite, package build; no re-record needed unless a successful-sample path changes.
## Remaining acceptance details

- An early Herdr version/start/core failure with no core running records only that subject's
  gap and lets other cells continue; a genuine failure to stop a core that did start still aborts
  as a cleanup failure with diagnostics. Do not hide real leaks by accepting every stop error.
- A successful load wait gets its own `--load-wait` budget without spending the combined startup
  and workload budget; startup plus workload must remain bounded together. A load timeout stays
  an environment failure. Exercise success after a long wait and failure/cleanup with focused
  production-path tests; test doubles must not require host load or a real Herdr server.
- Update DEVELOPMENT's subject list and deadline description (:593-594 at 8ebdd69), preserving
  the existing failure diagnostics. The former "failure paths only" observation describes the
  review baseline, not proof of the future fix: if the successful-sample path changes, follow
  the original acceptance and re-record the affected cohort with identities and environment.
- Reuse shared isolation/result owners; whole-workspace eon-test, affected bench/package proof
  and converge before landing. No product contract or publication change.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
# Note for eon-benchmarks-xl2bp.4 (Orbit throughput), from eon-benchmarks-xl2bp.2

The completion writer (`eon-bench write FILE --report REPORT`) bounds only its
wait for the status reply: it fails 60 s after writing `ESC[5n`, even while
other input arrives, and restores the terminal mode. Its write of FILE has no
deadline: if the terminal under test stops reading its PTY, `write_all`
blocks forever. In `floor --layer pty` the harness's reader covers this (60 s
of silence on the master kills the writer by its PID and fails the sample).
Suites that run the writer inside a terminal the harness does not read, such
as Orbit attached or detached and the reference terminals, need their own
deadline: either a harness-side timeout that kills the writer by exact PID,
or a write-side deadline in the writer (nonblocking stdout plus `poll`
for POLLOUT against a deadline). Decide in that bead which one owns it.

title: Record v0.2.0's benchmark results in beads, measured on the tree that ships
description:
## Why

Child of the benchmark epic eon-benchmarks-xl2bp; gates v0.2.0 (blocks eon-igae.9). Lucca,
2026-11-09: "we dont need to publish, we can fix this before pushing / we can save it only to

docs/benchmarks or on eonterm.com. This supersedes the 2026-11-07 decision to publish a results
page. The page itself (eon-bench rendering tables and SVG charts, the eonterm.com text) moved,
unchanged, to eon-benchmarks-xl2bp.21, outside the gate, for when Lucca chooses to publish.

Research and suite design: eon-benchmarks-xl2bp.1,
~/.cache/eon-agents/eon-bench-1-work/bead/ (04-recommended-suite.md, 05-children.md; the common
checks are at the top of 05-children.md).

## Goal

The numbers v0.2.0 ships with, recorded once on the tree that ships, so Lucca can judge the
release and a later page can cite them.

## Scope

In: after the performance gate work lands (eon-orbit-coalesce-gu13n and any follow-up beads Lucca
picks from eon-bah29's report), rerun the recorded suites on one candidate revision: Orbit
throughput (xl2bp.4), memory per terminal and per client (xl2bp.5, with Venus client memory from
xl2bp.18), the terminal comparison (xl2bp.6) and multiplexer overhead and per-window memory
(xl2bp.17), plus frame/idle results from now-gating xl2bp.10.
Final measurement follows selected cache/blink and remote frame/history changes too; its revision
must not predate output-path gate work. Post one results comment on eon-benchmarks-xl2bp: per metric, Eon's number, the
comparison numbers, direction, revision, machine, compositor, renderer, grid, scrollback, runs and
statistic; the kernel floor from xl2bp.2; "parser floor not recorded" unless xl2bp.3 has landed;
"latency not measured" unless xl2bp.11 or .12 proved a method (Lucca, 2026-11-07: no published
keystroke latency from a software probe alone). Name where Eon trails and the bead that addresses
it.

Evidence storage is settled by the overseer's 2026-11-09 decision under Lucca's "auto-decide":
raw archives live at /home/lucca/pjs/eon-evidence/<bead>/ outside agent cache, with archive SHA-256s
and result.json identities in the results comment. Already-pushed docs/benchmarks records/archives
stay as landed-change evidence; no new ones are added. Do not reopen the choice or use a retired
agent-cache path as the final evidence home.

Out: docs/benchmarks pages, SVG charts, eonterm.com text (eon-benchmarks-xl2bp.21); new suites.

## Acceptance

- One results comment on eon-benchmarks-xl2bp; every number in it traces to a recorded run
  (result.json path and SHA-256) at a named revision.
- That revision includes every gate change to Orbit's or Venus's output path; if one lands
  later, the affected suite is rerun before the cut.
- No new file under docs/benchmarks and no site change.

## Verification

Records only. Timed runs go through heavy.sh with a quiet window (REQUEST first), on isolated
roots, never Lucca's window.

title: Upgrade Orbit to Bend 2.0.40 and prove compiler compatibility
description:
## Why

Orbit pins Bend 2.0.37 at 234cb9b950800f20b15feafcb4ce2f43e76e7fae. Upstream v2.0.40, published 2026-11-06, adds checker corrections and checking optimizations worth evaluating on Orbit's shipped policy. A pin-only bump is unsafe: the worker assumes short File.read results, and its runtime arguments use the pre-2.0.38 convention.

Planning authorization: Lucca, 2026-11-07, after discussing the compiler bump and selective Bend expansion: "create and update the beads". This records the upgrade work; it approves no contract/law change, worker recovery mechanism, or wider language adoption.

## Evidence

- flake.nix:37-41 and :288-290 pin and assert the current compiler. flake.lock records its source identity.
- orbit/build.rs:28-50 invokes Bun, emits C, and compiles the worker with clang. nix/orbit-checks.nix:38-58 separately builds the mismatched test worker; :313-319 runs the proof gate.
- orbit/src/main.bend:94-98 calls File.read(input, 4096). orbit/src/host.rs:297-301 writes one short fact and waits for an answer. With v2.0.40's fill-until-max/EOF rule, those two sides appear to wait on each other; this is a source-based inference, not an observed failure on an upgraded build.
- orbit/src/host.rs:1758-1759 passes --threads 1. Since 2.0.38, compiled runtime options require +RTS ... -RTS.
- orbit/tools/step-proof.rs:1115-1176 parses error excerpts and expected/observed diagnostics to regenerate lemmas; newer checker diagnostics can affect regeneration even when committed proofs pass.
- orbit/docs/CRATES.md:141-161 owns the dependency decision and version/exit policy; orbit/docs/BEND.md owns pinned-version practices.
- Upstream target: v2.0.40 = 624dd9f4607cd29b0871a9b96d413bfb11e92f52, confirmed with git ls-remote on 2026-11-07. Read CHANGELOG.md, bend2/effs/file_read.c and bend2/base.bend at that revision. The line-read implementation currently makes byte-at-a-time reads: do not assume unchanged round-trip cost.
- Sources: https://github.com/bendlang/bend/releases/tag/v2.0.40 ; https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.40/CHANGELOG.md ; https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.40/bend2/effs/file_read.c .

## Contract and prerequisites

Preserve existing ORB-C1 through ORB-C17 behavior and wire identities; ORB-C12/C13 cover shutdown and management, and ORB-C14 owns native Darwin evidence. No new indexed contract is proposed. Read the applicable root/Orbit rules, orbit/docs/REFERENCES.md's Session policy in Bend route, HOST.md, BEND.md, CRATES.md and DEVELOPMENT.md before changing the dependency.

Record the exact-revision dependency/reference gate before code: compare retaining 2.0.37 with 2.0.40, compiler/Bun/clang identities, license and closure, compatibility findings, and a return-to-prior-pin path that preserves current Orbit behavior. Consult eon-n2m7 for trigger-based exit criteria and eon-fony for the unresolved recovery decision; neither authorizes changing failure semantics in this upgrade.

## Scope

In scope: flake.nix/flake.lock's Bend identity and assertion; minimal worker IO and runtime-argument adaptations; the mismatched-worker build/check path; proof-generator compatibility only where the new compiler requires it; focused regression coverage; relevant current-version documentation. Keep Bun/compiler/clang build- and check-time only, telemetry disabled, and package the generated worker through orbit/build.rs's existing recipe.

Out of scope: new laws or weakened proofs, EON/ORB/VEN contract edits without approval, UI changes, Venus/Runtime Bend adoption, a compiler fork, an owned C adapter, worker recovery, unrelated toolchain bumps, a new runtime protocol, and resuming legacy Orbit differential checks.

Portability disposition: neutral source/toolchain upgrade; independently establish compiled-worker and IO behavior on x86_64-linux and aarch64-darwin. A missing platform result remains an explicit gap rather than a compile-only success.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The exact 2.0.40 commit is pinned consistently; production and test workers use the same compiler recipe/identity.
- The compiled worker answers a short first fact and subsequent facts promptly on an open pipe; it does not wait for 4096 bytes or EOF. The intended runtime thread configuration is effective under the new option convention.
- Existing laws check without weakening; a property-targeted negative mutation fails at its intended law. A bounded regeneration exercise also succeeds on a scratch copy, demonstrating that proof tooling still understands the compiler.
- All affected Rust/Nix checks and real-PTY behavior pass on the exact candidate under the repository harness; native Darwin results and any remaining gap are recorded precisely.
- An interleaved comparison against this tree built with the previous Bend pin records proof/check time and memory, regeneration cost, and worker/PTY throughput under comparable low-load conditions. Investigate material regressions before acceptance; do not use the historical Rust Orbit table as today's baseline.
- Current-version docs match the accepted build and proof route. Refresh the installed profile only after the candidate is accepted, then verify an isolated fresh-session artifact without stopping or restarting live supervisors. Record exact proof and required independent review in this bead within the implementation commit.

## Implementation Notes

1. Rebaseline the live owner sources and upstream target; resolve short-line reading and runtime arguments using supported Base effects.
2. Make the smallest compatible pin/adaptation change. Extend the existing worker/real-PTY harness for a meaningful regression instead of adding a parallel test framework.
3. Exercise proofs and regeneration, then the affected delivery surfaces. Keep generated boundary/proof files generated by their owners.

## Verification

Use the shared runtime/build dependency route in docs/AGENT-RULES.md and Orbit's existing DEVELOPMENT.md harness: affected Rust suites through nix develop -c eon-test, Orbit fmt/clippy and affected Nix package/check surfaces. The compiled worker exchange, generator sensitivity and current-pin A/B observations are distinct falsifiers; pure proofs alone cannot cover changed IO/runtime behavior. Stop and record a blocked native platform proof if no suitable host is available; do not silently drop it.

## Stop Conditions

Stop for Lucca before a contract/law change, a compiler fork or native-adapter dependency, changed worker-fault semantics, or a material performance/support tradeoff. Stop on material owner drift or an out-of-scope requirement, and on the same verification failure twice after a reasonable fix attempt. Never touch a running Eon window or Orbit process to obtain proof.

## Maintenance Notes

This is one compiler-upgrade slice, with its compatibility fixes and exact proof kept together. It is separate from evaluating further Bend ownership. Existing worker-fault containment remains the accepted behavior; eon-fony owns any survival proposal. eon-n2m7 retains user approval of exit-trigger wording.
